name: Hallux sesamoid injury (sesamoiditis & fracture)
aka: pain under the big toe joint
populations: adolescent dancers, gymnasts and runners (58 young athletes, 51 of them female, in one series)
athletes with repeated forefoot loading and great-toe extension
football and other athletes after a hyperextension or axial-load injury
people with a bipartite sesamoid, where the cleft can be injured or mistaken for a fracture
summary: Pain under the 1st metatarsal head from the hallux sesamoids: sesamoiditis, stress fracture or acute fracture. Most settle with offloading, but recovery is slow and bipartite sesamoids can confuse the diagnosis.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Slow. In 58 young athletes, 89.8% of fractures were treated without surgery and the mean time to pain-free or cleared for sport was 161.4 days (about 23 weeks)

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Young athletes: 84.7% returned to sport. After sesamoidectomy in a systematic review: 94.4% returned, 90.0% to their previous level, at a mean of 11.8 weeks

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Focal tenderness over a sesamoid under the first metatarsal head, with pain on loading and on passive great-toe dorsiflexion; compare with the other foot

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Weightbearing radiographs with a sesamoid axial view; early MRI when pain persists; CT to confirm union. A bipartite medial sesamoid (12.7% of feet in one survey) can mimic or hide a fracture

keyFacts.label: Classification
keyFacts.value: No validated grading. Descriptive: sesamoiditis (poorly defined), stress fracture, acute fracture, nonunion, avascular necrosis and the bipartite variant

keyFacts.label: Load
keyFacts.value: The sesamoid complex transmits up to 50% of body weight and more than 300% during push-off

overview:
The two hallux sesamoids lie in the flexor hallucis brevis tendons under the first metatarsal head, within the plantar plate of the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint. They normally transmit up to 50% of body weight, and more than 300% during push-off [r1]. Because of these loads and anatomical variation, they are affected by acute fractures, stress fractures, nonunions, osteonecrosis, chondromalacia and a group of inflammatory conditions labelled sesamoiditis [r2]. 'Sesamoiditis' remains poorly defined, and symptoms are nonspecific pain on the plantar surface of the first metatarsal head [r3].

In a series of 58 patients aged 9–21 years with 59 sesamoid fractures, 83.1% were repetitive stress injuries rather than acute trauma, dancing (37.9%), running (13.8%) and gymnastics (13.8%) were the commonest sports, and 89.8% were managed without surgery [r4]. Treatment starts with an accommodative orthosis and immobilisation, and operations range from fixation and bone grafting to partial or complete sesamoidectomy for recalcitrant cases [r1,r2]. Most evidence is from case series, and a bipartite sesamoid can make diagnosis difficult [r5,r6].

epidemiology.text: No population incidence figures were identified in the sources reviewed. In a retrospective review at one children's hospital, 58 patients (51 females and 7 males, mean age 15.4 years, range 9–21) had 59 hallux sesamoid fractures over five years; dancing (37.9%), running (13.8%) and gymnastics (13.8%) were the most common sports, and 83.1% of fractures were stress injuries versus 16.9% acute traumatic injuries [r4]. A medial partite hallux sesamoid was present in 12.7% of 3994 feet in a Japanese population survey (10.0% in men and 13.7% in women), and it became less common with age [r6]. The medial sesamoid is frequently bipartite and the lateral occasionally so [r7]. One study states that up to 64–90% of sesamoid fractures heal with non-operative management [r8].

intrinsic: A bipartite or multipartite sesamoid, whose cleft can be injured or mistaken for a fracture; the medial sesamoid is frequently bipartite [r7,r6]
Adolescence and female sex in the youth series (51 of 58 patients were female), which may reflect participation in dance and gymnastics rather than sex itself [r4]
A medial partite sesamoid is associated with hallux valgus [r6]
A high-arched foot or a plantarflexed first ray that increases loading under the first metatarsal head (clinical observation; not tested in the sources reviewed)
extrinsic: Dance, running and gymnastics, which load the forefoot repeatedly with the great toe extended [r4]
High peak loads at push-off: the sesamoid complex can transmit more than 300% of body weight [r1]
Acute hyperextension or axial loading of the great toe, as in turf toe or a hard landing on the forefoot, which can fracture a sesamoid or separate a bipartite one [r7]
Sudden increases in training load, hard surfaces or thin forefoot cushioning (clinical observation; modifiable)

mechanism.summary: There are two mechanisms. The commonest in athletes is repetitive stress: the sesamoids take very high loads under the first metatarsal head at push-off (more than 300% of body weight), and repeated cycles produce a stress fracture or a painful, inflamed sesamoid [r1,r4]. The second is acute trauma: forced hyperextension of the great toe, or a hard axial load on the forefoot, can fracture a sesamoid or separate the synchondrosis of a bipartite sesamoid, sometimes together with a turf toe injury of the plantar plate [r7]. Which of the two sesamoids is injured depends on the loading pattern; in one nonunion series most fractures were in the tibial sesamoid [r9].
sequence: The athlete repeatedly loads the forefoot with the great toe extended, for example in relevé, sprinting and jump landings [r4,r1].
The sesamoids sit within the flexor hallucis brevis tendons beneath the first metatarsal head, raising it and increasing the lever arm of the flexors [r7].
At push-off they transmit more than 300% of body weight [r1].

Repetitive loading causes bone microdamage faster than it is repaired, so a stress reaction develops (the typical stress fracture sequence; most fractures in the youth series were stress injuries) [r4].
A fracture line forms in a normal sesamoid, or at the synchondrosis of a bipartite sesamoid [r5,r7].
If loading continues, healing is delayed, and a nonunion or avascular necrosis can follow; sesamoid nonunions need operative treatment in some patients [r2,r10].
The athlete has pain under the first metatarsal head with weightbearing and push-off, with tenderness over the sesamoid [r4,r3].

variants.name: Sesamoiditis
variants.description: A term for pain from the hallux sesamoids without a clear fracture, covering several inflammatory and overload conditions; it remains poorly defined, so imaging is needed to look for an underlying cause [r3,r11].

variants.name: Stress fracture
variants.description: The most common sesamoid fracture in young athletes (83.1% of 59 fractures), often after weeks of forefoot pain in dancers, runners and gymnasts [r4].

variants.name: Acute traumatic fracture
variants.description: Accounted for 16.9% of fractures in the youth series [r4]. It can follow forced hyperextension or a crush or landing injury and may coexist with a plantar plate injury [r7].

variants.name: Bipartite sesamoid injury
variants.description: The synchondrosis of a bipartite or tripartite sesamoid can be injured, and in one athlete a fracture of a bipartite medial sesamoid was treated as sesamoiditis for 12 months before MRI confirmed it [r7,r5]. Progressive diastasis of 3–5 mm on initial radiographs signalled injury in some athletes [r7].

variants.name: Nonunion and avascular necrosis
variants.description: Persistent pain and a fracture that does not unite; surgical options include fixation, bone grafting and sesamoidectomy [r2,r10].

variants.name: Infection (osteomyelitis)
variants.description: Seen mainly in people with diabetes or neuropathy: in a series of 24 patients with sesamoid osteomyelitis, 92% had diabetes and all had neuropathy [r12].

anatomy.text: The hallux sesamoids are paired ossicles embedded in the tendons of the flexor hallucis brevis (FHB) beneath the first metatarsal head, within the plantar plate. The medial (tibial) sesamoid is typically larger and sits more distal than the lateral (fibular) sesamoid. The flexor hallucis longus runs between them in its own sheath, and the abductor and adductor hallucis conjoin with the medial and lateral FHB heads [r7]. The sesamoids act as a fulcrum, elevating the first metatarsal head and increasing the leverage of the flexors [r7]. In normal gait the complex transmits up to 50% of body weight and more than 300% during push-off [r1]. Sesamoid blood supply and the course of the plantar digital nerve beside the tibial sesamoid are standard anatomy that is relevant to avascular necrosis and to numbness after surgery.

structures.name: Medial (tibial) sesamoid
structures.role: Larger, more distal sesamoid; takes load under the first metatarsal head and is more often involved in nonunion series [r7,r9]

structures.name: Lateral (fibular) sesamoid
structures.role: Smaller sesamoid on the fibular side; bipartition is less common than medial [r7]

structures.name: Flexor hallucis brevis tendon
structures.role: Encloses both sesamoids and inserts on the proximal phalanx with the plantar plate [r7]

structures.name: Plantar plate and sesamoid-phalangeal ligaments
structures.role: Capsuloligamentous restraint that resists dorsiflexion; injured in turf toe, which can coexist with a sesamoid fracture [r7]

structures.name: Flexor hallucis longus tendon
structures.role: Runs plantar to the metatarsal head between the sesamoids, flexing the great toe [r7]

structures.name: First metatarsal head
structures.role: Articulates with the sesamoids on its plantar surface; chondromalacia is described among sesamoid disorders [r2]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Sesamoid disorders include acute fractures, stress fractures, nonunions, osteonecrosis, chondromalacia and inflammatory conditions grouped as sesamoiditis [r2]. Under repetitive high loads, bone microdamage accumulates, a stress reaction develops and a fracture line can form. Because the sesamoids bear load at every push-off, the fracture is exposed to repeated stress during healing, so union can be slow or fail. Sesamoiditis is poorly defined, and imaging can show that pain originates from a fracture, avascular necrosis, infection, arthritis or a tumour rather than inflammation alone [r3].

Recovery is slow. In young athletes, the mean time from diagnosis to being pain-free or cleared for sport was 161.4 days [r4]. When a fracture does not unite, operative options (fixation with or without bone graft, or sesamoidectomy) usually succeed in the short term: union rates were 90.5–100% in a systematic review of 80 patients with nonunion, although the studies were few and of low quality [r10]. Sesamoidectomy carries its own risk: the complication rate was 22.5% in a systematic review of 196 feet [r13].

structures.name: Sesamoid bone (tibial more often than fibular)
structures.effect: Stress reaction, stress fracture, acute fracture, nonunion or avascular necrosis [r2,r4]

structures.name: Synchondrosis of a bipartite sesamoid
structures.effect: Can be injured or separate (diastasis 3–5 mm on initial radiographs in some athletes), and can be mistaken for a fracture [r7,r5]

structures.name: Plantar plate and FHB tendon
structures.effect: Can be sprained or torn with a hyperextension injury (turf toe), alongside the sesamoid [r7]

structures.name: Articular cartilage of the sesamoid and metatarsal head
structures.effect: Chondromalacia is described among sesamoid disorders [r2]

structures.name: Bursa and plantar soft tissue
structures.effect: Bursitis and callosities under the first metatarsal head can accompany sesamoid pain (clinical observation)

muscles.name: Flexor hallucis brevis and longus
muscles.effect: Pain inhibition and avoidance of push-off weaken great-toe flexion; strength is retested before loading (clinical reasoning).

muscles.name: Abductor and adductor hallucis
muscles.effect: They insert into the sesamoid complex; imbalance after a medial injury can cause traumatic hallux valgus [r7], although hallux valgus angle changes after sesamoidectomy were not significant in one review [r13].

muscles.name: Gastrocnemius–soleus and peroneus longus
muscles.effect: Disuse atrophy in a boot reduces push-off power; peroneus longus plantarflexes the first ray, and both are rebuilt before running and jumping (clinical reasoning).

muscles.name: Intrinsic foot muscles and hip extensors
muscles.effect: Maintain with cross-training during offloading (clinical reasoning).

cellular.description: Repeated loading creates microdamage faster than remodelling can repair it (typical bone stress sequence).
Marrow oedema and periosteal and trabecular reaction; pain on loading (typical).
A haematoma forms and inflammatory signals recruit repair cells.
Cartilage then woven bone bridges the gap, but repeated push-off loads can delay union; nonunion occurs in some patients [r10].
Lamellar bone replaces woven bone. In young athletes, pain-free or cleared status took a mean of 161.4 days [r4].

systems.effect: A medial partite sesamoid is associated with hallux valgus, and the first ray, arch and hallux alignment shape the load on the sesamoids [r6].
Avascular necrosis is a recognised sesamoid disorder, and a poor blood supply is one explanation for slow or failed union (standard anatomy; clinical reasoning) [r2].
Pain under the first metatarsal head alters push-off and gait. Numbness and neuropathic symptoms occurred after arthroscopic sesamoidectomy, so the plantar digital nerves need care [r14].

Stress-type sesamoid fractures in adolescent female dancers and gymnasts should prompt a screen for low energy availability and bone health (clinical convention; not tested in the sources reviewed) [r4].
Long recovery (a mean of 161.4 days in young athletes) is hard on dancers, gymnasts and runners and can lead to early, unsafe return [r4].

grading.system: Descriptive diagnostic categories (no validated grading system)

grades.description: Plantar first metatarsal head pain attributed to the sesamoids without a defined fracture. The term remains poorly defined, so image to look for fracture, avascular necrosis, infection or arthritis [r3,r11].
grades.prognosis: Conservative measures are first line in most cases [r15]; initial treatment almost always involves an accommodative orthosis [r1]

grades.description: A fracture from repeated loading, usually after weeks of forefoot pain; 83.1% of fractures in a young athlete series [r4].
grades.prognosis: Mean time to pain-free or cleared was 161.4 days; 84.7% returned to sport [r4]

grades.description: A fracture after hyperextension, a landing or direct trauma; 16.9% of fractures in the youth series, sometimes with a turf toe injury [r4,r7].
grades.prognosis: Up to 64–90% of sesamoid fractures heal with non-operative management in one report [r8]

grades.description: A fracture or sesamoid that fails to heal or loses its blood supply, with persistent pain [r2,r10].
grades.prognosis: Surgery usually succeeds in the short term: union 90.5–100% in a systematic review of 80 patients, with 6.5% complications and 6.5% reoperations [r10]

grades.description: A normal variant (medial partite sesamoid in 12.7% of feet) rather than an injury, but its cleft can be injured or mistaken for a fracture [r6,r5].
grades.prognosis: After arthroscopic grafting of nonunions, the two patients with congenitally distinct sesamoids had poor outcomes in a series of 11 [r9]

timeframes.summary: Recovery is long. In 58 young athletes, the mean time to pain-free or cleared for sport was 161.4 days [r4]. After surgery, union took a mean of 2.9 months with arthroscopic grafting, and temporary joint fixation was removed at 8 weeks after CT showed healing; return to sport followed at 5.3 months and 80 days respectively [r9,r8].

healing.description: Offload with an orthosis or boot and cross-train; a typical protective phase for a stress or acute fracture (clinical convention).
Callus and woven bone bridge the fracture; graduated weightbearing in a rigid-soled shoe once symptoms and imaging allow (typical bone healing).
Pain-free or cleared status was reached at a mean of 161.4 days in young athletes [r4].
Strength, load tolerance and sport-specific work are consolidated; nonunion work-up if pain persists (typical).

milestones.label: Union after temporary first MTP fixation
milestones.note: Removal of the construct at 8 weeks after CT-confirmed healing in 32 patients [r8]

milestones.label: Return to sport after temporary first MTP fixation
Mean time to pain-free or cleared (young athletes, mostly non-operative)
Return to sport after arthroscopic bone grafting

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based and slow. In a series of 58 young athletes, 84.7% returned to sport and the mean time to pain-free status or clearance was 161.4 days [r4]. After sesamoidectomy, 94.4% returned to sport (90.0% to their previous level) at a mean of 11.8 weeks in a systematic review [r13]. After arthroscopic bone grafting of nonunions, return took 5.3 months [r9]. No validated return-to-sport (RTS) criteria were identified.

symptoms: Gradual pain under the first metatarsal head (the ball of the big toe), worse with weightbearing, push-off, running and jumping [r3,r4]
Sudden pain after a landing, hyperextension injury or crush injury (acute fracture) [r4,r7]
Pain on forced plantarflexion of the great toe in one athlete with a bipartite sesamoid fracture, and a feeling of a bruise under the joint [r5]
Swelling and stiffness of the first MTP joint, with reduced push-off power
Pain that lasts for months despite treatment as 'sesamoiditis' (consider fracture, bipartite injury or necrosis) [r5,r15]
signs: Focal tenderness over the medial or lateral sesamoid on direct palpation under the first metatarsal head [r3,r15]
Pain on passive great-toe dorsiflexion and on resisted plantarflexion (clinical observation)
Swelling or bruising under the joint, callus or bursitis, and an antalgic gait with reduced toe-off
Tenderness that moves with the sesamoid when the great toe is flexed and extended (clinical observation)
Plantar plate laxity on the vertical Lachman test if a turf toe injury coexists [r7]

subjective: Onset: gradual (repetitive stress) or acute (landing, hyperextension, crush) [r4]
Sport and demands: dance (relevé, pointe), running, gymnastics, football; recent changes in training load, footwear or surface [r4]
Site and behaviour of pain: plantar first metatarsal head, worse with push-off and relieved by rest; night pain or constant pain
Duration and previous treatment: a long course treated as sesamoiditis should prompt imaging [r5,r15]
Previous foot injury or hallux valgus; menstrual history, diet and bone health in adolescents and female athletes (stress fracture screen; clinical convention)
Diabetes, neuropathy or a plantar ulcer (infection and avascular necrosis) [r12]
observation: Swelling, bruising, callus and bursitis under the first metatarsal head
Hallux alignment (valgus, varus) and first ray position; foot posture (cavus or flat)
Gait: antalgic with an avoided toe-off
Footwear fit, rigidity and cushioning; skin integrity and any plantar ulcer
palpation: Medial and lateral sesamoids separately, under the first metatarsal head, with the great toe in neutral and then flexed [r3]
Plantar plate and FHB tendon: tenderness distal to the sesamoids suggests plantar plate injury (turf toe), and tenderness proximal to them suggests an FHB strain [r7]
First MTP joint line, collateral ligaments and the metatarsal head
FHL tendon behind the first metatarsal head and the medial plantar digital nerve for nerve irritation
rangeOfMotion: First MTP dorsiflexion and plantarflexion compared with the other foot: pain at end-range dorsiflexion stretches the sesamoid complex
Ankle dorsiflexion (calf tightness raises forefoot load; clinical reasoning)
strength: Resisted great-toe flexion (FHB and FHL): pain and weakness are expected early
Single-leg heel raise: tolerance and height, once the foot can bear load
Intrinsic foot strength (short-foot) and peroneus longus
neuro: Sensation over the plantar medial digital nerve to the hallux and the dorsum of the great toe
Neuropathy screen if there is a plantar ulcer or diabetes [r12]
functional: Gait barefoot and in rigid-soled shoes
Single-leg hop, only when pain-free and cleared
Dancers: relevé and demi-pointe tolerance; runners: running gait on a treadmill (late)

specialTests.name: Direct sesamoid palpation with great-toe movement
specialTests.purpose: Localise pain to a sesamoid and distinguish it from the metatarsal head, the joint and the plantar plate
specialTests.procedure: With the patient seated and the foot relaxed, press under the first metatarsal head on the medial sesamoid and then on the lateral sesamoid. Passively flex and extend the great toe and note whether the tender point moves with the sesamoid [r3].
specialTests.positive: Focal sesamoid tenderness that moves with the great toe. No sensitivity or specificity data were identified in the sources reviewed.

specialTests.name: Passive great-toe dorsiflexion (end-range loading)
specialTests.purpose: Reproduce sesamoid pain through the plantar plate and FHB
specialTests.procedure: Passively dorsiflex the first MTP joint to end range and compare with the other foot.
specialTests.positive: Plantar pain at end range; limited range suggests joint or plantar plate involvement (clinical reasoning). No accuracy figures were identified.

specialTests.name: Resisted great-toe plantarflexion (FHB test)
specialTests.purpose: Test the FHB and the sesamoid complex under load
specialTests.procedure: Stabilise the interphalangeal joint in neutral and resist MTP flexion at the proximal phalanx; compare sides [r7].
specialTests.positive: Pain at the sesamoid or weakness compared with the other side. No accuracy data were identified.

specialTests.name: Vertical Lachman test of the first MTP joint
specialTests.purpose: Exclude a plantar plate rupture (turf toe) that may coexist
specialTests.procedure: Stabilise the first metatarsal and apply anterior and posterior force to the proximal phalanx, feeling for dorsal or plantar translation [r7].
specialTests.positive: Excess translation suggests plantar plate injury; see the turf toe page. No accuracy figures were identified.

specialTests.name: Single-leg heel raise and hop (late)
specialTests.purpose: Check load tolerance at the end of rehabilitation
specialTests.procedure: Single-leg heel raise to fatigue, then single-leg hop in place and forward, once pain-free and cleared.
specialTests.positive: Pain at the sesamoid or an inability to match the other side. No accuracy data were identified.

clinicalRules.name: Image when pain persists
clinicalRules.description: Persistent pain under the first metatarsal head after a course of conservative care should not be labelled sesamoiditis without imaging; early consideration of MRI and discussion with a musculoskeletal radiologist is recommended in one review [r15]. In one athlete, a fracture of a bipartite sesamoid was treated as sesamoiditis for 12 months before MRI confirmed it [r5].

clinicalRules.name: Fracture or bipartite sesamoid?
clinicalRules.description: Compare with the other foot. A bipartite sesamoid is a normal variant (medial partite sesamoid in 12.7% of feet), and fracture can mimic or hide within it; MRI helps when radiographs are equivocal [r6,r5]. Diastasis of 3–5 mm on initial radiographs signalled injury to a bipartite sesamoid in some athletes [r7].

clinicalRules.name: Stability and plantar plate check
clinicalRules.description: A hyperextension mechanism needs a vertical Lachman test and comparison weightbearing views, because a sesamoid fracture can coexist with a plantar plate rupture and sesamoid retraction [r7].

outcomeMeasures.name: Visual analogue scale (VAS) pain
outcomeMeasures.use: Used before and after sesamoidectomy and bone grafting [r13,r9]

outcomeMeasures.name: Foot Function Index (FFI), Foot and Ankle Outcome Score (FAOS) and Japanese Society for Surgery of the Foot (JSSF) score
outcomeMeasures.use: Patient-reported and clinician-rated function after surgery and injection [r16,r17,r9]

outcomeMeasures.name: AOFAS ankle–hindfoot score
outcomeMeasures.use: Used in the sesamoidectomy systematic review (mean 92.7) [r13]

outcomeMeasures.name: Return to sport rate and time to pain-free
outcomeMeasures.use: The main outcomes in the youth and operative series [r4,r9]

imaging.modality: Weightbearing radiographs (AP, lateral and sesamoid axial) with comparison of the other foot
imaging.indication: First-line for all suspected sesamoid injuries [r7]
imaging.findings: A fracture line or fragmentation; a bipartite sesamoid has a smooth cleft (a normal variant in 12.7% of feet). Compare with the other side; diastasis of 3–5 mm on initial views can mean injury to a bipartite sesamoid [r7,r6].

imaging.indication: Persistent pain with non-diagnostic radiographs, suspected stress fracture, avascular necrosis, plantar plate injury or infection; early consideration is recommended [r15,r3]
imaging.findings: Marrow oedema, a fracture line, avascular necrosis, chondral damage and soft-tissue injury; helpful when 'sesamoiditis' is suspected but poorly defined [r3,r5].

imaging.indication: Assessing union, nonunion and bone detail before surgery; used to confirm healing before removal of fixation [r8,r16]
imaging.findings: Fracture gap, sclerosis, fragmentation and bridging bone; union was assessed with radiographs and CT after grafting [r16].

imaging.indication: Bursitis, tendon problems and guided injection when fracture is not suspected (clinical reasoning)
imaging.findings: Soft-tissue findings only; it cannot exclude a sesamoid fracture. No accuracy figures were identified in the sources reviewed.

differentials.name: Turf toe (first MTP plantar plate injury)
differentials.distinguishing: A hyperextension mechanism, tenderness distal to the sesamoids, a positive vertical Lachman test and sesamoid retraction; it can coexist with a sesamoid fracture [r7].

differentials.name: Flexor hallucis brevis or longus tendinopathy or strain
differentials.distinguishing: Pain with resisted flexion and tenderness proximal to the sesamoids or behind the metatarsal head rather than directly over the sesamoid [r7].

differentials.name: Hallux rigidus or first MTP arthritis
differentials.distinguishing: Stiffness, dorsal osteophytes and pain at end-range dorsiflexion rather than focal plantar sesamoid tenderness (standard clinical teaching).

differentials.name: Gout or inflammatory arthritis of the first MTP joint
differentials.distinguishing: A hot, red, swollen joint without a loading history; urate and aspiration help (standard clinical teaching).

differentials.name: Sesamoid osteomyelitis or plantar ulcer
differentials.distinguishing: Diabetes or neuropathy with a plantar ulcer or sinus; MRI shows marrow change, and outcomes are poor with a 63% complication rate [r12].

differentials.name: Metatarsal stress fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Pain over the first or second metatarsal shaft or neck rather than directly under the sesamoids.

differentials.name: Morton's neuroma
differentials.distinguishing: Burning web space pain between the toes with a positive squeeze test rather than pain under the first metatarsal head.

differentials.name: Intractable plantar keratosis or bursitis under the first metatarsal head
differentials.distinguishing: A callus or a soft-tissue swelling directly under the sesamoid with normal bone on imaging (clinical observation).

redFlags: Open wound, severe deformity, dislocation of the great toe, or a cold or pale toe: send to emergency.

Plantar ulcer, hot red swollen toe, fever, or diabetes or neuropathy with great-toe pain: suspect osteomyelitis and arrange urgent medical and surgical review; isolated sesamoidectomy for osteomyelitis had a 63% complication rate [r12].
Instability on the vertical Lachman test or sesamoid retraction on weightbearing views: a plantar plate rupture needs surgical review (see turf toe) [r7].

Persistent pain after about 3 months of adherent non-operative care (clinical convention), or a nonunion or avascular necrosis on imaging: refer for orthopaedic foot and ankle review, because many nonunions need operative treatment [r10,r2].
Pain that has been labelled sesamoiditis for months without imaging: arrange MRI, because a bipartite sesamoid fracture can be missed [r5,r15].

After surgery: fever, wound redness or discharge, calf pain or breathlessness, new numbness over the plantar great toe, or a drifting hallux (valgus, varus or cock-up): arrange urgent review [r14,r7].

management.principles: Diagnose the specific lesion (stress fracture, acute fracture, bipartite injury, avascular necrosis, plantar plate injury) rather than accept 'sesamoiditis', using early MRI when pain persists [r15,r3]. Conservative measures are first line in most cases: an accommodative orthosis and immobilisation, with cross-training and graduated loading [r15,r1]. In young athletes 89.8% of fractures were treated without surgery, and 84.7% returned to sport, but recovery averaged 161.4 days [r4]. Surgery is for recalcitrant cases and includes fixation, bone grafting and partial or complete sesamoidectomy, with a high return to sport but real complications [r1,r13]. Preserve a sesamoid pole where possible [r7]. Evidence is from case series and reviews with no randomised trials, so involve the athlete, set realistic timelines and explain the options.

medical.name: Accommodative orthosis and immobilisation (non-operative care)
medical.description: Initial treatment almost always involves an accommodative orthosis [r1]; conservative management with orthotics and immobilisation is described in a review of hallux sesamoid disorders [r2]. In the youth series, 89.8% of fractures were treated conservatively and 84.7% of patients returned to sport [r4]. One report states that 64–90% of sesamoid fractures heal with non-operative management [r8].

medical.name: Fluoroscopically guided corticosteroid injection (selected cases)
medical.description: A review suggests that, where fracture and avascular necrosis have been ruled out, injection under fluoroscopic guidance may avoid surgery [r15]. Steroid is avoided in fracture or avascular necrosis, and cortisone is not advised near the plantar plate in turf toe [r7]. No controlled trial was identified.

medical.name: Orthobiologic injections (platelet-rich plasma, concentrated bone marrow aspirate)
medical.description: In three teenage athletes with recalcitrant injuries, a single PRP treatment was followed by return to impact activities at 6–9 weeks, but other management factors probably contributed [r18]. In 15 patients treated with concentrated bone marrow aspirate, FAOS and VAS improved at a mean of 20.1 months, 8 of 11 athletes returned to play (7 to the previous level) and 3 patients (20%) needed further treatment [r17]. Case series without controls.

medical.name: Fixation, bone grafting or temporary joint fixation for nonunion or recalcitrant fracture
medical.description: A systematic review of 80 patients with nonunion reported union in 90.5–100%, with complication and reoperation rates of 6.5% each, from six low-quality studies [r10]. In 10 patients, screw fixation with autogenous bone grafting gave union in all by 3 months and improved FFI from 72.3 to 8.2 at 12 months (two had hardware removed) [r16]. Arthroscopic grafting in 11 patients gave union at a mean of 2.9 months and return to sport at 5.3 months, but the two patients with congenitally distinct sesamoids had poor outcomes [r9]. Temporary first MTP fixation in 32 patients gave a 94% union rate and return to sport at a mean of 80 days; at a mean of 10 years, 2 had asymptomatic nonunion [r8].

medical.name: Partial or complete sesamoidectomy (including arthroscopic)
medical.description: In a systematic review of 10 studies (196 feet), VAS fell from 6.5 to 1.2, the mean AOFAS ankle–hindfoot score was 92.7 and 94.4% of athletes returned to sport (90.0% to their previous level) at a mean of 11.8 weeks; hallux valgus angle changes were not significant, but the complication rate was 22.5% and the revision rate 3.0% [r13]. In 14 arthroscopic cases, VAS fell from 75.4 to 14.3 mm, but complications included wound pain, numbness and residual discomfort [r14]. Preserve one pole of a fragmented sesamoid if possible, and transfer abductor hallucis into the defect if both poles are excised [r7].

medical.name: Analgesia and short-term immobilisation
medical.description: Simple analgesia, ice and a rigid-soled shoe or boot for the first weeks (clinical convention).

physio.name: Education and load management
physio.description: Explain the lesion, the long timeline (a mean of 161.4 days in young athletes) and why great-toe extension loading is reduced; manage training volume [r4].

physio.name: Offloading orthoses, footwear and taping
physio.description: An accommodative orthosis [r1]; typical designs include a cut-out or pad under the first metatarsal head, a rigid-soled or rocker shoe and, for dancers, taping and adjusted footwear to limit great-toe dorsiflexion (clinical convention). No controlled trial of a specific orthosis was identified.

physio.name: Cross-training and proximal strengthening
physio.description: Cycling or swimming without great-toe loading, plus hip, core, calf and intrinsic foot work during offloading (clinical convention).

physio.name: Graduated weightbearing and impact loading by criteria
physio.description: Progress on clinical findings and imaging (union where there is a fracture), not time alone. In operative series, CT was used to confirm healing before loading or hardware removal [r8,r16].

physio.name: Great-toe flexor, calf and first-ray strengthening
physio.description: Progressive FHB and FHL, calf raise and peroneus longus work once weightbearing is allowed, then push-off and jump loading (clinical convention).

physio.name: Bone health screening in stress-type fractures
physio.description: Screen for low energy availability, menstrual disturbance and low bone density in adolescent and female athletes with stress-type sesamoid fractures (clinical convention; not tested in the sources reviewed).

physio.name: Continuing sport or dance on a painful sesamoid
physio.description: A fracture needs offloading to unite (clinical reasoning), and nonunion often needs surgery [r10,r2].

physio.name: Treating persistent pain as sesamoiditis without imaging
physio.description: A fracture of a bipartite sesamoid was treated as sesamoiditis for 12 months before MRI confirmed it, and a review advises early MRI [r5,r15].

education: The sesamoids are two small bones under the ball of the big toe that act like pulleys for the toe flexors. They take huge loads, and they can bruise, crack or become sore.
Most sesamoid fractures heal without surgery, but healing is slow: in young athletes it took about five months on average. Plan for a long recovery.
Offloading is the main treatment: a padded insert, a stiff-soled shoe or a boot, and activities that do not load the big toe. Keep fit with swimming, cycling and upper-body and core work.
Some people are born with a sesamoid in two pieces. This is normal and can look like a fracture on X-rays, so your clinician may compare your other foot and order an MRI.
If a fracture does not heal, surgery to fix, graft or remove the sesamoid usually works. Removal returns most athletes to sport but can cause complications such as numbness or toe drift.
Do not return to dance, running or jumping until your clinician agrees, because pushing through pain can stop the bone healing.

rehab.overview: Progression is criteria-based and follows the diagnosis (stress fracture, acute fracture, sesamoiditis, nonunion or post-operative care). Always follow the surgeon's instructions after surgery. Evidence for specific rehabilitation protocols is minimal, so the program below follows clinical reasoning and the time courses reported in the literature: a mean of 161.4 days to pain-free or cleared in young athletes [r4], and return to sport at about 80 days to 5.3 months after surgery [r8,r9]. Move on when pain, tenderness and function criteria are met (and imaging if there is a fracture). Dosages are typical clinical ranges, not prescriptions from a single source.

stages.name: Offload & settle
stages.timeframe: Weeks 0–6 (longer after a fracture or surgery)
goals: Offload the sesamoid and settle pain
Protect the fracture or the repair
Maintain proximal strength and cardiovascular fitness
precautions: Follow the boot or orthosis and weightbearing plan exactly [r1]
Do not stretch the great toe into dorsiflexion

exercises.name: Ankle range of motion
exercises.cues: Keep the great toe relaxed and protected

exercises.name: Double-leg glute bridge
exercises.cues: Weight through the heels; the forefoot stays relaxed

exercises.name: Side-lying hip abduction (clamshell)
exercises.cues: Keep the pelvis still and the foot protected

exercises.name: Quadriceps sets and straight-leg raise
exercises.cues: Lock the knee and keep the foot unloaded

exercises.name: Upper-body ergometer or swimming (pull buoy)
exercises.cues: No push-off against the wall with the great toe

progressionCriteria: Resting pain at or below 2/10 and tenderness reducing
Imaging confirms healing where a fracture was shown (clinician decision) [r8,r16]

stages.name: Graduated loading
goals: Return to full weightbearing in a rigid-soled shoe
Restore ankle motion and calf control
precautions: Use an offloading orthosis and rigid-soled or rocker shoe
Keep pain at or below 3/10 and settled the next day (clinical convention)
Avoid forced great-toe dorsiflexion and push-off

exercises.name: Graded weight-shift and walking in a rigid-soled shoe
exercises.dosage: 5 × 1 min building to 20–30 min walks, daily
exercises.cues: Roll through the foot; do not push off the great toe

exercises.name: Seated calf raise
exercises.cues: Press through the forefoot within pain limits

exercises.name: Short-foot (arch) activation
exercises.cues: Shorten the foot without curling the toes

exercises.name: Single-leg balance in a stiff-soled shoe
exercises.cues: Soft knee and quiet trunk

exercises.name: Cycling with the foot placed under the arch
exercises.cues: Load through the arch, not the ball of the foot

progressionCriteria: Full weightbearing without a limp and with pain at or below 2/10
No tenderness over the sesamoid on palpation
Clinician confirms healing or stability (and imaging where a fracture was present)

stages.name: Strength & push-off control
goals: Restore calf, FHB and foot strength
Tolerate push-off loading in a rigid-soled shoe
precautions: Progress calf loading slowly because heel raises load the sesamoids
Stop if tenderness, swelling or push-off pain returns

exercises.name: Double-leg calf raise, then single-leg
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10–12 building to single-leg 3 × 8–12, every second day
exercises.cues: Even weight over the first and fifth toes; stop at the first twinge

exercises.name: Single-leg calf raise
exercises.dosage: 3 × 8–12, 3 s up and 3 s down, every second day
exercises.cues: Full range with the weight over the first and second toes

exercises.name: Step-up and controlled step-down
exercises.cues: Keep the pelvis level and the knee over the second toe

exercises.name: Resisted great-toe flexion with a band or towel
exercises.cues: Press the toe down while the heel stays on the floor

exercises.name: Single-leg balance with perturbation
exercises.cues: Keep the arch active and the great toe flat

progressionCriteria: Single-leg calf raise × 15 with pain at or below 2/10 and equal height to the other side
Walks 30–40 min and jogs 10 min without sesamoid pain
No tenderness on palpation or on end-range dorsiflexion
Clinician (and imaging where relevant) confirms healing

stages.name: Return to impact & sport
stages.timeframe: Weeks 16–26+ (criteria-based; mean pain-free or cleared 161.4 days in young athletes [r4])
goals: Return to running, jumping and cutting
Dancers: relevé, demi-pointe and pointe progression
Return to team training and competition
Plan footwear, orthosis and load monitoring
precautions: Add volume in steps and avoid rushing; push-off loading too early risks delayed union
Do not return to competition while the sesamoid is tender or swollen

exercises.name: Walk–run program
exercises.dosage: 1 min run / 2 min walk for 20 min, 3 times a week, adding running every 1–2 sessions (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Quiet landings and an even push-off

exercises.name: Single-leg hop in place, forward and lateral
exercises.cues: Soft landing and stick for 2 s

exercises.name: Jump landing and rebound drills
exercises.cues: Land on the whole foot, hips and knees bent

exercises.name: Dancers: graded relevé progression
exercises.dosage: Double-leg relevé 3 × 10, then demi-pointe and single-leg over 4–8 weeks (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Weight over the first and second toes; no sinking into the forefoot

exercises.name: Planned then reactive change of direction
exercises.dosage: 2 sessions a week, increasing speed and angle
exercises.cues: Plant on the whole foot, then rotate

exercises.name: Graded team training
exercises.dosage: Partial then full training over 2–3 weeks
exercises.cues: Share the plan with the coach or dance teacher and monitor pain and swelling

progressionCriteria: Full training for at least 2 weeks with pain at or below 1/10 and no next-day flare
Single-leg hop distance and calf-raise capacity at or above 90% of the other side (clinical convention)
No tenderness over the sesamoid; union confirmed where a fracture was present
Athlete, coach or teacher and clinician agree on the return

criteria: No validated return-to-sport (RTS) criteria were identified for hallux sesamoid injuries; the criteria below reflect clinical convention and the operative series [r4,r8]
No tenderness on palpation of the sesamoids and no pain on end-range great-toe dorsiflexion
Radiographic or CT evidence of union (or surgeon sign-off) where a fracture, nonunion or surgery was involved [r8,r16]
Pain-free running, jumping and push-off at or below 1/10 with no swelling or next-day flare
Calf, hop and balance performance at or above about 90% of the other side (clinical convention)
Dancers: pain-free relevé, demi-pointe and pointe work in the appropriate footwear; full training for at least 2 weeks with a footwear and orthosis plan agreed with the athlete, coach and clinician
tests: Palpation of each sesamoid and end-range dorsiflexion
Resisted great-toe flexion strength by dynamometer
Single-leg heel raise repetitions and height
Single-leg hop tests (single, triple, side) with pain rating
Radiographs or CT as directed by the surgeon
Weekly training volume and next-day pain and swelling log

prognosis: Most sesamoid fractures in young athletes do well with conservative treatment, but recovery is prolonged. In 58 patients with 59 fractures, 89.8% were treated without surgery, 84.7% returned to sport, and the mean time to pain-free or cleared status was 161.4 days [r4]. One report states that 64–90% of fractures heal non-operatively [r8]. Fractures that do not unite often need surgery. In a systematic review of 80 patients, union rates were 90.5–100% after operative treatment of nonunion, with complication and reoperation rates of 6.5% each; sesamoidectomy remained the most reliable salvage procedure [r10]. After sesamoidectomy, 94.4% of athletes returned to sport at a mean of 11.8 weeks, with a complication rate of 22.5% and a revision rate of 3.0% [r13]. Bipartite sesamoids are less predictable: the two patients with congenitally distinct sesamoids had poor outcomes after arthroscopic grafting [r9]. Evidence is mostly small retrospective series.
prevention: No prevention trials were identified. The commonest group affected is young dancers, gymnasts and runners, so early recognition of forefoot pain is the key [r4].
Increase training load gradually, particularly in adolescents, and avoid sudden increases in relevé, jumping and sprint volume (clinical convention).
Review footwear, cushioning and surfaces, and consider an accommodative insert for athletes with recurrent sesamoid pain and a high-arched foot (clinical observation) [r1].

Screen adolescent female athletes for low energy availability and bone health, because most patients in the youth series were female and most fractures were stress injuries (clinical convention) [r4].
Do not train through persistent plantar great-toe pain: image early, because a fracture needs offloading to heal [r15,r10].
clinicalPearls: Think of a sesamoid fracture in dancers, gymnasts and runners with pain at the base of the big toe, especially adolescent females; 83.1% of fractures in one youth series were stress injuries [r4].

A bipartite sesamoid (medial partite sesamoid in 12.7% of feet) can mimic or hide a fracture. Compare with the other foot and get an MRI if radiographs are equivocal; one fracture of a bipartite sesamoid was treated as sesamoiditis for 12 months [r6,r5].
Set expectations early: the mean time to pain-free or cleared was 161.4 days in young athletes, even though 89.8% avoided surgery [r4].
Do not accept 'sesamoiditis' as a final diagnosis. Persistent pain should lead to MRI and a specific diagnosis (fracture, avascular necrosis, plantar plate injury, infection) [r15,r3].
Always test the plantar plate (vertical Lachman, sesamoid retraction on weightbearing views) after a hyperextension injury, because a turf toe injury can coexist with a sesamoid fracture [r7].
Surgery returns most athletes to sport (94.4% after sesamoidectomy) but the complication rate was 22.5%, and congenitally distinct sesamoids did worse after grafting, so counsel carefully [r13,r9].

animation.title: How a hallux sesamoid injury happens

forces.label: Push-off loads the ball of the foot
More than 300% of body weight through the sesamoids

captions.text: A runner (or a dancer or gymnast) repeats push-offs many thousands of times.
At push-off the weight shifts to the ball of the foot and the big toe.
The two sesamoids under the first metatarsal head take most of that load.
In walking they carry about half the body weight, and in push-off much more.
With rising training load, the bone can be loaded faster than it repairs.
Zooming into the big toe joint, viewed from the inner (medial) side.
The two sesamoids lie in the flexor hallucis brevis tendons, under the first metatarsal head.
They act as a fulcrum, raising the metatarsal head and increasing the leverage of the toe flexors.
At push-off, the ground force drives up through the sesamoids.
With repeated loading, microdamage builds up in the sesamoid bone.
A stress reaction develops: pain under the ball of the big toe with push-off.
If loading continues, a fracture line forms. Most heal with offloading, but slowly.
A bipartite sesamoid has a smooth natural cleft that can be mistaken for a fracture.
Healthy bone: an ordered network of osteocytes and mineralised collagen in balance.
Loading: each push-off loads the sesamoid and stimulates adaptation.
Microdamage: repeated cycles create tiny cracks faster than normal.
Remodelling removes damaged bone faster than new bone is laid down, so the bone is briefly weaker.
Stress reaction: marrow oedema and periosteal reaction appear, and it hurts to load.
Stress fracture: a crack runs through the sesamoid if loading continues.
Healing is slow in a sesamoid: a mean of about 5 months in young athletes, and some fractures do not unite.
